utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- but I should also note, at least with respect to the English translation, I believe the scenarios -- the word "scenarios" on line 18, the second time, is actually the tabs, if I'm not mistaken. Perhaps my learned colleague can clarify that. But we would ask that the map that the witness marked be specifically admitted into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Scenarios 1 through 19 should -- instead of "scenarios" it should be "tabs." Has the Defence any objection regarding the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. President. I just should like to make a clarification regarding some of the numbers. DH2053 ID, Mr. Registrar said it was a table but there's also a part of a book, which is part of the same number. The same applies to DH1642. Mr. Registrar mentioned that there was a table, but the table is accompanied also by an extract from a book from which the table is taken. Also, under tab 3 this document is also part of DH1978. It is the work table used by the witness in which he refers to the 15 scenarios and he deals with the distances, the altitudes, and his conclusions regarding the first test of optical visibility. That is the table to which I made some corrections following the objections of the Prosecution. That is, scenario 14 on this table is the same as scenario 7, and scenario 15 thus becomes scenario 14; scenario 16 is the same as scenario 7; and scenario 17 becomes scenario 15. Mr. President, this table is also a part of DH1978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This corrected table, have you made the corrections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this should be done on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will make those corrections and I will provide the registrar with the table. But the CD has already been given to the registrar with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Registrar, you need to give us a number for the Prosecution exhibit, that is, the map, and another number for the CD, which needs to be identified.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The map identified by the witness today is Prosecution Exhibit P952. The CD given to the registrar a moment ago is admitted as DH2060. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of what has been said on the -- under the reservation that the Defence will provide a corrected table of tab 3. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. There's a final important comment to make. The witness did not mention to which situation the scenarios related. But to facilitate the work of the Chamber, we would like to say to which witness each of these scenarios relates, and for that purpose I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us go into private session. But I'll first give -- I'll give the floor to Mr. Mundis after that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, I give the floor to the Defence, who wish to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I take the floor concerning a filing that we have just received. It's a letter dated the 4th of March, 2005 entitled "Deputy Registrar's submission regarding the issue of translation of documents for the Defence." Mr. President, this letter, I would have preferred to have it avoided, but it has been filed. When the Chamber adjourned proceedings for a week, I prepared some arguments to submit to the Chamber so as to avoid the Defence being blamed for this week of interruption in the proceedings. Having thought the matter over, I thought that we were all acting in good faith and there was no point in arguing the matter and that everyone would understand; however, that was not the case, and we have a written submission by the Assistant Registrar of the Tribunal. It has been filed in accordance with Rule 33(B) of the Rules. I think 33(B) of the Rules does not allow the Assistant Registrar to write such a submission and to blame a Defence team and thereby calling in question its neutrality and impartiality in the proceedings. This is only one matter. I will come back to it later in detail. Secondly, the filing, which I still haven't had time to analyse fully, in our view omits many elements, and I will limit myself to two such elements. First of all, this question of translation for the Defence team is a problem that exists for a long time now, and even before the trial started I personally made a lengthy expose to explain the situation. The situation that we -- which we explained - it was in the month of November of the year when the trial started - has still not been resolved. We still don't have in this Tribunal a policy which would say which documents should be translated in support of a Defence team in the submission of its case. The situation, as you know, Mr. President, is quite different from the Prosecution, who can count on, in addition to the Registrar's service, their own translation services. Also, a year before the trial we proposed a plan to the Registrar, which was adopted in other cases, to have translations done by people who would cost less, and we established a budget, and this whole matter was rejected. More recently, in December last year and on several occasions before that but most specifically in December, we told the Registrar that the translation services are doing everything they can and we, too, are doing everything we can to avoid any problems during the proceedings. I think there were more than a thousand documents, and the sum of money required to avoid any interruption of the proceedings for a week was minimal compared with the cost of interrupting a trial for a week. But the managers of this Tribunal do not look at the costs. Certainly some translations could have been made before this became a problem. I will stop there, Mr. President, to tell you simply that we will respond to the submissions filed by the Assistant Registrar. We will respond in detail, and clearly that is the only case we can do, and we will do it and in detail. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for this clarification. We haven't still familiarised ourselves with that document, so I cannot respond on that level. But personally - and I think the other Judges share my opinion - the week when we had an interruption, the interruption was made at the request of the Prosecution because the Prosecution, to prepare their cross-examination, wanted to have in English all the documents that you have in B/C/S. So it wasn't you that asked for the interruption; it was the Prosecution, which indicated that they needed to have all the documents in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: So we held a hearing which mobilised us. And if it hadn't been held, we would have to have held it later. So we didn't waste time. Also, in my personal name, it is my opinion that the Defence is entitled to having documents translated, as well as the Prosecution, and the Judges too, in order to be able to judge, we need to have documents translated. This is an absolute necessity. So obviously we're going to study the document of the Registry. But let me tell you, Mr. Bourgon, that you are not a person that is to be blamed because it was not you who asked for the interruptions; it was the Judges who felt that in order to allow the Prosecution to be able to cross-examine, as is their right, to have few -- a few days' break. And, of course, you will respond to the document. Rule 33(B) does say that "The Registrar may inform in writing --" I assume it is the Chamber that they informed, but there's no indication in 33(B) to inform us. And in any case, we will have your response to this, and I wish to underline that at the very beginning of the trial you did draw the attention of the Chamber and the Registry to this question of translation. So you fully highlighted all the problems of translation in good time. And in spite of the difficulties that you have encountered and the Prosecution, we were at times forced to deal with documents in B/C/S so as not to allow the proceedings to suffer any delays, and thanks to your cooperation we were able to forge ahead with the proceedings. And as I said today, it is the 191st sitting. And this will certainly be one of the longest at this Tribunal. So we will for our part study the Registrar's document, and we have always supported both the Prosecution and the Defence with respect to the need for translations of documents. And the very fact that there is no translation in realtime involves additional work for everyone. We need to mark documents for identification, we'll have to go back to them, et cetera, et cetera. And of course it would be desirable to have all the documents translated in time. The Rules require that all documents of Rule 66 and 68 be disclosed to the Defence, that they be translated into the language of the accused, and of course either into English or French. That is the legal obligation which the Registry has to fulfil. However, as we are in an adversarial system, it is quite normal for the Defence, when its case comes up, to provide all the documents they feel are necessary and to have them translated by the Registry as the Defence does not have a personal translation service at their disposal. This is a matter that can be usefully addressed by the Council of -- the Commission of the Defence Counsels. In the ten minutes left, does anyone wish to address some other matter which may not be of not such importance? Nothing to address, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mrs. Residovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, of course, all documents addressed to the Registry or the Chamber need to be translated, either into English or French. That is quite obvious. I'm just waiting for the order to be given to me by the registrar before adjourning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I may not have been quite clear. As we are in open session, to make myself clearer regarding my proposal, perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let's go into PS, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, today's hearing is adjourned. I invite everybody to be here tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. And just a remark: This week we will be sitting in the afternoon every day, including even Friday. Thank you very much.
